title: Public-sector reform ideas diffuse faster than the institutional capacity and political conditions needed to sustain them
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11457, What Works for Public Sector Reform in Africa? Preliminary Evidence on New Public Management Reforms in World Bank Projects
geography: Sub-Saharan Africa; World Bank-financed public-sector reform projects implemented between 2010 and 2023, supplemented by four qualitative case studies

observations.period: 2010-2023; World Bank-financed public-sector reform projects in Sub-Saharan Africa

denominator.unit: reviewed World Bank-financed public-sector reform project corpus

npm_prevalence.value: more than one-third of reviewed projects included at least one New Public Management intervention

full_implementation.unit: percent of New Public Management interventions fully implemented

reform_types.value: performance-based incentives and greater autonomy, including performance-based public financial management, agencification, and performance-based pay

mechanism.value: policy diffusion and project adoption can outpace administrative capability, implementation resources, and political conditions

observations.method: Review of project design, implementation, and performance information for World Bank-financed public-sector reform projects, supplemented by qualitative cases.
observations.uncertainty: The corpus concerns World Bank-financed projects and intervention coding; full implementation is not equivalent to improved public services, and project performance data may not represent all public-sector reforms in the region.
observations.subgroup: Public administrations, central agencies, sector ministries, reform units, civil servants, political executives, donors, and citizens receiving public services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Partial implementation may reflect realistic sequencing, financing interruptions, or measurement limitations rather than intrinsic failure; some reforms may produce value before formal completion.

observations.period: 2010-2023; variation across New Public Management reform types

denominator.unit: comparative performance assessment of coded reform types

comparative_performance.value: performance-based public financial management reforms performed comparatively better than agencification and performance-based pay reforms

authority_rewiring.value: agencification and performance-based pay attempt more directly to rewire authority and incentives inside bureaucracies and are more challenging to implement

design_constraint.value: mixed outcomes are linked to insufficient attention to institutional capacity, implementation constraints, and political-economy dynamics

service_route.value: reform design affects whether public management changes become reliable service delivery, staff discretion, feedback, and citizen-facing remedy

observations.method: Cross-reform comparison using project design, implementation, and performance information, with interpretation through institutional and political-economy constraints.
observations.uncertainty: Comparative performance can reflect reform selection, project context, implementation support, baseline capacity, and measurement differences rather than the intrinsic superiority of one reform family.
observations.subgroup: Financial-management agencies, autonomous agencies, civil servants subject to performance pay, ministries, reform sponsors, frontline providers, and service users.
observations.counterinterpretation: Performance-based financial management may appear easier to implement because it fits existing budget routines or has more measurable outputs; agencification and pay reforms may require longer horizons or complementary civil-service changes.

observations.period: Four qualitative cases; reform sustainability in fragile and neo-patrimonial contexts

case_contexts.value: Madagascar, Benin, Burkina Faso, and Burundi

sustainability.value: New Public Management reforms are particularly difficult to sustain in fragile and neo-patrimonial contexts

political_economy.value: reform durability depends on authority, incentives, coalitions, institutional legitimacy, and context-specific implementation rather than imported design alone

legitimacy_route.value: citizens experience reform through continuity, responsiveness, staff discretion, administrative burden, and whether public institutions correct failure

observations.method: Four qualitative in-depth case studies used to interpret project-level patterns and sustainability conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The cases are illustrative and not a representative sample of fragile or neo-patrimonial states; qualitative mechanisms do not estimate average effects or causal impact.
observations.subgroup: Fragile administrations, political and bureaucratic coalitions, reform champions, frontline civil servants, donors, and citizens navigating public services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Fragility and neo-patrimonialism are broad contextual labels that can obscure variation, local agency, successful reform pockets, and the role of external financing or conflict shocks.

related_sources.claim: Bibliographic record and abstract for WPS11457, including project prevalence, 40 percent implementation, reform-type variation, and four case studies.
Official World Bank document record and metadata for WPS11457.

boundary: This record adds reform-design-to-state-capacity conversion as an institutional and legitimacy mechanism. It is not a representative evaluation of all African public-sector reform, not evidence that full implementation improves citizen outcomes, and not proof that New Public Management reforms are universally ineffective or that one reform family always dominates.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank PDF and abstract record were reviewed for project prevalence, 40 percent full implementation, reform-type performance differences, design and political-economy constraints, four country cases, sustainability claims, and project-level evidence boundaries.
